HORMONES AND PLANT MOVEMENTS

  • This deficiency may also cause the thyroid gland to enlarge, leading to a condition known as goitre. An excess production of iodine can result in hyperthyroidism, where the thyroid becomes overactive and produces too much thyroxine.

Parathyroid Gland

  • The parathyroid glands are four small glands located behind the thyroid gland in the neck.
  • The main role of the parathyroid glands is to regulate the level of calcium in the blood and bones. They do this by producing a hormone called parathyroid hormone (PTH).
Diabetes Insipidus is caused when the body produces too much urine and is not able to retain water (due to lack of ADH/Vasopressin).

Adrenal Gland

  • It is a cap-like structure located above both the kidneys.
  • It releases Adrenal hormone → also known as "Flight-or-Fight hormone".
  • It increases the blood pressure, heart rate, and metabolism in response to stress level.
  • Deficiency causes: Addison's disease (a rare chronic condition in which your adrenal glands don't produce enough of the hormones cortisol (stress hormone) and aldosterone).
Q. Can you recall the function of saliva in digestion?

Major Exocrine Glands

Sweat Glands

  • They release sweat, a secretion, onto the skin's surface through ducts.

Salivary Glands

  • These glands are a type of exocrine gland located in and around the oral cavity. They produce saliva, a fluid essential for digestion, lubrication, and protection of the mouth.

Liver

  • The liver is positioned in the upper right portion of the abdomen, beneath the diaphragm. It is a large organ.
  • The liver is responsible for numerous functions, including filtering blood, producing bile for digestion, metabolizing proteins, carbohydrates, and fats, and storing glycogen and vitamins.

Stomach

  • The stomach helps break down food by squeezing it (mechanical) and mixing it with acids (HCl) and enzymes (chemical). Ghrelin released by stomach stimulates appetite hence it is known as "Hunger Hormone".

Heterocrine/Mixed Glands

  • A heterocrine gland is a gland that functions as both an endocrine gland and an exocrine gland.

Examples of heterocrine glands:

Pancreas

  • Pancreas releases both hormones and enzymes (covered in digestive system) thus acting as a mixed gland.
  • It is the second largest gland of our body.

Hormones released by pancreas:

  • Islets of Langerhans: These are cells scattered throughout the pancreas.

Types:

  • α-Cells: Produces Glucagon → converts Glycogen to Glucose through Glycogenolysis.
  • β-Cells: Produces Insulin → converts Glucose to Glycogen through Glycogenesis. Diabetes Mellitus is caused when not enough insulin is produced by the body.

Gonads

  • They are the primary reproductive organs.

Gonads include:

  • Testes: In male → releases testosterone hormone.
  • Ovary: In female → releases Estrogen (responsible for female characteristics) and Progesterone (it supports menstruation and maintains pregnancy).
The Atrial wall of human heart secretes a very important peptide hormone known as: ANF (Atrial Natriuretic Factor). ANF helps regulate the blood pressure.

PLANT HORMONES AND MOVEMENTS

HormonesFunction
AuxinElongation of stem
GibberellinGermination or flowering in plants
CytokininCell division
Abscisic AcidStress hormone that inhibits growth
EthyleneGaseous hormone responsible for fruit ripening

Plant Movements

  • Plant movements are of two types: Tropic Movements and Nastic Movements.
  1. 1. Tropic Movements: They are directional and occur in response to stimuli like light, gravity, water, and chemicals. They can be positive or negative.
  • (a) Positive Tropism: When a plant part moves towards the stimulus, it's considered positive tropism.
  • (b) Negative Tropism: When a plant part moves away from the stimulus, it's considered negative tropism.

Types of Tropic Movements:

  1. 1. Phototropism: Movement of plant in response to light. Movement in response to light. Shoots bend towards light (positive), while roots bend away from it (negative).
  2. 2. Geotropism: Movement in response to gravity. Roots grow downwards towards the gravity (positive growth), while shoots grow upwards away from the gravity (negative growth).

HORMONES AND PLANT MOVEMENTS

Phototropism diagram: Barrier shielding the plant from the sun; Plant bending towards light (Positive Phototropism); Auxin moves to the dark side to make cells in that area grow faster; Positive Phototropism; Negative Phototropism

Geotropism diagram: Positive Geotropism (root); Negative Geotropism (shoot); downward growth

  1. 3. Hydrotropism: Movement in response to water. Roots grow towards water sources (positive growth).

Hydrotropism diagram: Negative hydrotropism (Shoot grows away from water); Positive hydrotropism (Root grows straight towards water); Porous clay pot; Water; High moisture content

  1. 4. Chemotropism: Movement in response to chemicals. E.g. The movement of pollen tubes towards the ovary during fertilization.

Chemotropism diagram: Pollen; Generative nucleus; Tube nucleus; Pollen tube; Extending tip of pollen tube (growing towards ovule in response to the chemical stimulus) (Positive Chemotropism); Ovule (secretes chemical stimulus); Sperm nuclei (n); Tube nucleus degenerates

  1. 2. Nastic Movements: They are non-directional movement of a plant part in response to an external stimulus, such as light, touch, or temperature.

Types:

  • (a) Photonastic Movement: The non-directional movement of plant part, usually flower petals, in response to changes in light intensity.
  • (b) Thigmonastic Movement: A non-directional response of plant or fungus to touch or vibration.

Photonastic Movement diagram: During the day the flower opens; At night it closes

Thigmonastic Movement diagram: The fly lands on the leaves; The leaves close and the fly is trapped.

REPRODUCTION

Reproduction

  • Reproduction is the biological process by which living organisms produce offspring to continue their species.
  • It is not essential for individual's survival, but is crucial for survival of a species.

Reproduction tree: Asexual Reproduction / Sexual Reproduction

Asexual Reproduction Vs Sexual Reproduction

Asexual ReproductionSexual Reproduction
Only one parent plant is involvedBoth male and female parents are involved
Occurs in unisexual plantsOccurs in bisexual plants
Occurs in lower plantsOccur in higher plants
Genetic similarity is commonly seen hereGenetic diversity is commonly seen here
Reproductive organs are not presentFully developed reproductive parts are present

Metagenesis: A type of life cycle in which one generation of plants or animals reproduce asexually, followed by sexually reproducing generation i.e., some individual of species are diploid and some are haploid.

  • E.g. Obelia.

ASEXUAL REPRODUCTION

Types of Asexual Reproduction

  1. 1. Binary Fission
  • It is a process of asexual reproduction in which a unicellular organism divides into two organisms.
  • It is common only in unicellular organisms. E.g. Amoeba.
  1. 2. Multiple Fission
  • It is a process of asexual reproduction in which the nucleus divides multiple times, and the cytoplasm divides later to form many new daughter cells.
  • Many offsprings are produced. E.g. Plasmodium (malarial parasite).
  1. 3. Fragmentation
  • It is a process of asexual reproduction in which the body breaks into pieces, and each fragment grows into a new organism.
  • It occurs in simple multicellular organisms. E.g. Spirogyra (green algae), Rhodophyte (red algae), and sea anemone.
  1. 4. Budding
  • It is a process of asexual reproduction in which a new organism develops from a bud or outgrowth on the parent organism.
  • A small bud forms on the parent body due to cell division. It grows and detaches to form a new organism.
  • It occurs in simple multicellular and unicellular organisms. E.g. Hydra (multicellular) and Yeast (unicellular).
  1. 5. Regeneration
  • It is a process of asexual reproduction in which a new organism develops from a part of the original organism. E.g. Planaria, Hydra.
Note: In higher organisms like lizards, tail regeneration does not form a new organism → just a part.
